triage.name: Steatotic Liver Disease
triage.reason: Common incidental abnormal liver enzymes or imaging finding; diagnosis reachable by history (alcohol, metabolic risk factors), exam, labs and imaging, with important distinctions between alcohol-associated and metabolic causes.

demographics: More common in adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes; prevalence rises with age
In the US, MASLD is more prevalent in Hispanic and non-Hispanic White populations than in non-Hispanic Black populations
Alcohol-associated liver disease is more common in men, but women develop liver injury at lower levels of alcohol intake
Children and adolescents can develop MASLD, usually in the setting of obesity

risk_factors.text: Metabolic syndrome (high blood pressure, high triglycerides, low HDL, elevated fasting glucose)
Heavy or long-standing alcohol use (for alcohol-associated liver disease)
Certain medications (corticosteroids, some cancer chemotherapies, amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen)
Female sex for alcohol-associated injury at lower intake
Genetic variants (e.g., PNPLA3) and family history

family_history: Steatotic liver disease or cirrhosis in a first-degree relative
Type 2 diabetes in a first-degree relative
Obesity or dyslipidemia in a first-degree relative
social_history: High intake of processed foods, sugar-sweetened beverages, or fructose
Lower socioeconomic status and food insecurity
exposures: Occupational or environmental exposure to hepatotoxins (e.g., carbon tetrachloride, vinyl chloride)
Herbal or dietary supplements with potential hepatotoxicity

chief_complaints.text: I feel tired all the time
I have a dull ache in my upper right belly
My doctor said my liver tests were abnormal
I don't have any symptoms, it was found on a scan

hpi.onset: Insidious; often discovered incidentally on routine blood work or imaging
hpi.duration: Months to years; may be present for a long time before detection
hpi.progression: Usually stable or slowly progressive; most patients remain asymptomatic, but some develop progressive fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis
hpi.location: Right upper quadrant or epigastric region when discomfort is present
hpi.timing: Intermittent or constant; not typically related to meals

associated_symptoms.text: Right upper quadrant discomfort or fullness
Mild jaundice (yellowing of eyes or skin)
Weight gain or difficulty losing weight

pertinent_negatives: Use of hepatotoxic medications or supplements
Swelling of the abdomen or legs
Known viral hepatitis or autoimmune liver disease

atypical.how_it_differs: Usually asymptomatic and detected during evaluation for obesity or incidentally on labs; abdominal pain can be more prominent.
More likely to have advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis at presentation and may present with complications such as ascites or encephalopathy.
missing_classic_features: Absence of signs of chronic liver disease

atypical.how_it_differs: Often have metabolic syndrome and more severe steatohepatitis; symptoms may be attributed to obesity rather than liver disease.
Higher risk of advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis; may have normal ALT despite significant disease.
Steatotic liver disease may be pre-existing and can worsen during pregnancy; must be distinguished from acute fatty liver of pregnancy, which is a different emergency.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, often overweight or obese with central adiposity; no distress
general.moderate: Well-appearing but fatigued; central obesity; may have acanthosis nigricans or other metabolic stigmata
general.severe: May appear chronically ill with signs of advanced fibrosis or portal hypertension (spider angiomas, palmar erythema, muscle wasting)
general.critical: Ill-appearing with decompensated cirrhosis: jaundice, ascites, confusion, or asterixis

findings.finding: Elevated BMI (overweight or obese) with increased waist circumference

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant and percuss the liver span

Percuss for shifting dullness and test for a fluid wave
Inspect the upper trunk, face, and arms

labs.caveat: ALT is often only mildly elevated or even normal in steatotic liver disease; a normal ALT does not exclude significant fibrosis. ALT > AST favors MASLD.
An AST/ALT ratio above 1 suggests alcohol-associated liver disease or advanced fibrosis; in MASLD the ratio is usually below 1.
Supports alcohol use or biliary involvement but is nonspecific; can be elevated by many medications.
Mild elevation can occur; marked elevation should prompt evaluation for biliary obstruction or infiltrative disease.
Usually normal or only mildly elevated until advanced disease; higher values suggest cirrhosis or another cause.
Low albumin indicates synthetic dysfunction and suggests advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis.
Thrombocytopenia is an early clue to portal hypertension and advanced fibrosis; a low platelet count should trigger fibrosis assessment.
Prolongation reflects impaired synthetic function in advanced disease.
Fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dL indicates prediabetes and 126 mg/dL or higher supports diabetes, both part of the metabolic criteria.
Documents prediabetes or diabetes as a cardiometabolic criterion.
Hypertriglyceridemia is a cardiometabolic criterion and often accompanies insulin resistance.
Low HDL is a cardiometabolic criterion; the reference lower limits are 40 mg/dL in men and 50 mg/dL in women.
Part of global cardiovascular risk assessment rather than the liver diagnosis itself.
Mildly elevated ferritin is common in steatotic liver disease as an acute-phase reactant; marked elevation or high transferrin saturation should prompt evaluation for hemochromatosis.
Hypothyroidism is associated with steatotic liver disease and is a treatable contributor to abnormal liver tests.

Thrombocytopenia or cytopenias suggest portal hypertension or advanced fibrosis

First-line test to confirm hepatic steatosis and screen for cirrhosis, splenomegaly, or biliary disease

confirmatory.why: Noninvasive confirmation of steatosis and staging of fibrosis, which determines prognosis and referral

confirmatory.test: MRI liver with proton density fat fraction and MR elastography
confirmatory.why: Confirms and quantifies steatosis and fibrosis when elastography is unavailable or discordant
confirmatory.only_if: elastography is unavailable or results are discordant

confirmatory.why: Definitive diagnosis and staging when noninvasive tests are discordant or another cause is suspected
confirmatory.only_if: noninvasive testing is nondiagnostic or an alternative cause such as autoimmune or drug-induced liver disease is suspected

supporting.only_if: ferritin is elevated or transferrin saturation is high

supporting.only_if: thrombocytopenia, low albumin, or signs of cirrhosis are present

Not part of the liver workup

Does not assess hepatic fat or fibrosis and rarely changes management

decision_points: Quantify alcohol use with a validated tool before labeling disease as metabolic; both can coexist
Screen for advanced fibrosis with a noninvasive test (FIB-4 or elastography) in everyone with steatosis, since symptoms and aminotransferases do not predict stage
If FIB-4 or elastography is indeterminate or high, refer to hepatology and consider biopsy or MR elastography
Check pregnancy status before imaging or biopsy in anyone who could be pregnant
Evaluate competing causes (viral hepatitis, autoimmune, drug-induced, iron overload, Wilson disease in younger patients) when the picture is atypical

criteria.name: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)
criteria.summary: Hepatic steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor, without another clear cause and without heavy alcohol use. Cardiometabolic factors include overweight or obesity, prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and metabolic syndrome.
items: Hepatic steatosis on imaging or histology
At least one cardiometabolic criterion (overweight/obesity, prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL, or metabolic syndrome)
No heavy alcohol use and no other competing cause of liver disease

criteria.name: Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD)
criteria.summary: Hepatic steatosis in the setting of chronic heavy alcohol use, with typical laboratory findings such as an AST/ALT ratio above 1 and elevated GGT. It is the earliest stage of alcohol-related liver injury and can progress to alcoholic hepatitis and cirrhosis.
items: History of chronic heavy alcohol use
Hepatic steatosis on imaging or histology
AST/ALT ratio above 1 and often elevated GGT

differential.name: Alcohol-associated liver disease
differential.why_considered: Hepatic steatosis with abnormal liver enzymes in a patient who drinks alcohol; overlaps heavily with metabolic steatotic liver disease and the two often coexist.
differential.trigger: Any patient with hepatic steatosis who reports more than moderate alcohol use, or whose AST/ALT ratio is above 1.

history: Chronic heavy or binge alcohol use, quantified with a validated tool
Drinking pattern temporally related to liver enzyme abnormalities
Prior episodes of alcohol withdrawal or alcohol-related medical problems
exam: Signs of chronic liver disease out of proportion to metabolic findings
Tremor, tachycardia, or other features of alcohol use disorder
labs: Elevated total bilirubin and INR in alcoholic hepatitis
imaging: Hepatic steatosis on ultrasound or CT
Coarse echotexture or nodular contour suggesting advanced fibrosis
Transient elastography showing higher stiffness than expected for metabolic disease alone

differential.name: Chronic hepatitis C
differential.why_considered: Chronic viral hepatitis can cause mild transaminase elevation and is a known contributor to steatosis and fibrosis.
differential.trigger: Any patient with abnormal liver enzymes and risk factors for blood-borne infection, or with unexplained fibrosis.

history: History of injection drug use, blood transfusion before screening, or other percutaneous exposure
Known prior hepatitis C exposure or incarceration
exam: Usually no specific findings; may have signs of chronic liver disease if advanced
labs: Positive hepatitis C antibody with detectable HCV RNA
ALT and AST elevation that may fluctuate
Thrombocytopenia or low albumin if cirrhotic
imaging: Steatosis and fibrosis on ultrasound or elastography

differential.name: Chronic hepatitis B
differential.why_considered: Chronic hepatitis B can present with incidentally abnormal liver tests and hepatic steatosis, and is a treatable cause of chronic liver disease.
differential.trigger: Abnormal liver enzymes in a patient from a high-prevalence region, with household contacts, or with prior percutaneous exposure.

history: Birth in or travel to a high-prevalence region
Household or sexual contact with a person with hepatitis B
Prior injection drug use or hemodialysis
exam: Usually normal; signs of chronic liver disease only if advanced
labs: IgM anti-HBc if acute flare suspected
imaging: Steatosis and fibrosis on ultrasound or elastography

differential.name: Hemochromatosis
differential.why_considered: Iron overload can cause hepatic steatosis, elevated transaminases, and cirrhosis, and is easily missed if iron studies are not checked.
differential.trigger: Elevated ferritin with high transferrin saturation, or a family history of iron overload.

history: Family history of hemochromatosis or early-onset liver disease
Arthralgias, fatigue, or skin darkening
Diabetes or hypogonadism
imaging: Increased hepatic iron on MRI T2* or R2* sequences

differential.name: Wilson disease
differential.why_considered: A treatable inherited disorder of copper metabolism that can present with hepatic steatosis and abnormal liver tests, especially in younger patients.
differential.trigger: Liver disease in a patient under 40, or any patient with unexplained liver disease plus neuropsychiatric symptoms.

history: Younger age at presentation
Family history of liver disease or movement disorder
Neuropsychiatric symptoms such as tremor, mood changes, or school decline
labs: Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with low haptoglobin
imaging: Basal ganglia changes on brain MRI in neurologic disease

differential.name: Drug-induced liver injury
differential.why_considered: Many medications and supplements cause steatosis, elevated transaminases, or a mixed injury pattern that mimics steatotic liver disease.
differential.trigger: Temporal relationship between a new medication or supplement and abnormal liver tests, or jaundice with rising enzymes.

history: New medication, herbal product, or supplement in the weeks to months before presentation
Known hepatotoxic agents such as amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen, valproate, or corticosteroids
Fever, rash, or eosinophilia with some agents
exam: Rash or fever suggesting a hypersensitivity reaction
labs: ALT and AST elevation that may be marked
Eosinophilia or autoantibodies in some patterns
imaging: Normal or nonspecific findings on CT or MRI

differential.name: Primary biliary cholangitis
differential.why_considered: A chronic cholestatic liver disease that can present with fatigue and abnormal liver tests, and may coexist with steatosis.

history: Middle-aged woman with fatigue and pruritus
Dry eyes and dry mouth suggesting sicca symptoms
Family history of autoimmune disease
labs: Elevated alkaline phosphatase out of proportion to aminotransferases
Elevated total bilirubin in advanced disease

differential.name: Autoimmune hepatitis
differential.why_considered: An immune-mediated liver disease that can present with fatigue, abnormal liver enzymes, and hepatomegaly, and can be mistaken for steatotic liver disease.

history: Younger or middle-aged woman
Other autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease or celiac disease
Fluctuating or relapsing symptoms
labs: Elevated ALT and AST, often marked
Positive antinuclear antibody or anti-smooth muscle antibody

differential.name: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
differential.why_considered: An inherited cause of chronic liver disease that can present with abnormal liver tests and steatosis, especially in younger patients.

history: Family history of early emphysema or liver disease
Younger age at presentation
Smoking-related emphysema
exam: Signs of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Signs of chronic liver disease if advanced
labs: Abnormal alpha-1 antitrypsin phenotype or genotype

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Hypothyroidism is associated with steatotic liver disease and can cause fatigue, weight gain, and mild transaminase elevation.

history: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, and weight gain
Prior thyroid surgery or radioactive iodine
Family history of thyroid disease
exam: Dry skin, bradycardia, delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4
imaging: Thyroid ultrasound findings depending on cause

severity.mild: Simple hepatic steatosis without significant inflammation or fibrosis; asymptomatic or mild fatigue, normal or mildly elevated aminotransferases, and no evidence of advanced fibrosis on noninvasive testing.
severity.moderate: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis or alcohol-associated steatohepatitis with inflammation and early fibrosis (F1–F2); may have fatigue, right upper quadrant discomfort, and persistent enzyme elevation.
severity.severe: Advanced fibrosis (F3–F4) or compensated cirrhosis; may have thrombocytopenia, low albumin, splenomegaly, or signs of portal hypertension without overt decompensation.
severity.critical: Decompensated cirrhosis with ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, or hepatorenal syndrome; or acute-on-chronic liver failure with jaundice, coagulopathy, and multi-organ dysfunction.

red_flags.meaning: Hepatic encephalopathy and decompensated liver disease; needs urgent evaluation and hospitalization.
Variceal bleeding from portal hypertension; a life-threatening emergency.

red_flags.finding: Rapidly increasing abdominal girth or new lower extremity edema
red_flags.meaning: Ascites from decompensated cirrhosis; evaluate for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

red_flags.finding: Fever with abdominal pain in a patient with known ascites
red_flags.meaning: Possible spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; perform diagnostic paracentesis.

red_flags.finding: Thrombocytopenia or low albumin with elevated INR
red_flags.meaning: Advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis with synthetic dysfunction; refer to hepatology.

red_flags.finding: Marked transaminase elevation with rising bilirubin
red_flags.meaning: Acute liver injury or superimposed hepatitis; evaluate for drug toxicity, viral hepatitis, or ischemic injury.

complications.name: Progression to cirrhosis
clues: Coarse echotexture or nodular contour on imaging

complications.name: Hepatocellular carcinoma
clues: New liver lesion on surveillance ultrasound

complications.name: Ascites and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
clues: Ascitic fluid neutrophil count above 250 cells/mm3

complications.name: Hepatorenal syndrome
clues: Rising creatinine in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites
Lack of response to volume expansion

special_populations.differences: Usually asymptomatic and detected during evaluation for obesity or incidentally on labs; abdominal pain can be more prominent. Weight management and family lifestyle changes are the mainstay.
More likely to have advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis at presentation and may present with complications such as ascites or encephalopathy. Polypharmacy increases the risk of drug-induced liver injury.

Steatotic liver disease may be pre-existing and can worsen during pregnancy. Must be distinguished from acute fatty liver of pregnancy, which is a different emergency with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, and rapid progression.
Higher risk of advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis; may have normal ALT despite significant disease. Screen for fibrosis with noninvasive testing regardless of enzyme levels.

Often have metabolic syndrome and more severe steatohepatitis; symptoms may be attributed to obesity rather than liver disease. Weight loss of 7–10% of body weight can improve steatohepatitis and fibrosis.
Dose adjustments and avoidance of hepatotoxic medications are needed; vaccination against hepatitis A and B is recommended.

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink in a typical week, and has that changed recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Quantify with a validated tool; heavy or binge use points to alcohol-associated liver disease, while little or no use supports MASLD. Both can coexist.

key_questions.question: Have you been told you have diabetes, prediabetes, high blood pressure, or high cholesterol?
key_questions.looking_for: Cardiometabolic risk factors that are required to label steatotic liver disease as metabolic dysfunction-associated.

key_questions.question: Has your weight changed recently, and how much do you weigh now compared with a few years ago?
key_questions.looking_for: Overweight or obesity, central adiposity, or rapid weight loss; both weight gain and rapid loss can drive steatosis.

key_questions.question: What medicines, supplements, vitamins, or herbal products do you take?
key_questions.looking_for: Hepatotoxic agents such as corticosteroids, amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen, valproate, or herbal supplements that could explain the liver findings.

key_questions.question: Do you have any discomfort or fullness in your upper right belly?
key_questions.looking_for: Dull right upper quadrant ache or fullness; often absent because the disease is usually asymptomatic.

key_questions.question: How is your energy level? Do you feel tired all the time?
key_questions.looking_for: Fatigue or malaise, the most common symptom when any is present.

key_questions.question: Have you noticed yellowing of your eyes or skin, dark urine, or pale stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Jaundice or cholestatic symptoms suggesting advanced disease or an alternative cause such as biliary obstruction.

key_questions.question: Have you had swelling of your belly or legs, vomiting of blood, or black stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Ascites, variceal bleeding, or other signs of decompensated cirrhosis that need urgent evaluation.

key_questions.question: Any confusion, trouble concentrating, or excessive sleepiness?
key_questions.looking_for: Hepatic encephalopathy; altered mental status in liver disease is an emergency.

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had liver disease, cirrhosis, or early emphysema?
key_questions.looking_for: Inherited causes such as hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

key_questions.question: Have you ever had hepatitis, a blood transfusion, or injected drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk factors for chronic hepatitis B or C, which can cause steatosis and fibrosis.

key_questions.question: How much physical activity do you get, and what does a typical day of eating look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Sedentary lifestyle and high intake of processed foods or sugar-sweetened beverages that contribute to metabolic disease.

reasoning_points: Hepatic steatosis is confirmed on imaging (bright liver on ultrasound) or histology, often found incidentally.
The history quantifies alcohol use with a validated tool to separate metabolic from alcohol-associated disease, recognizing that both can coexist.
At least one cardiometabolic criterion is documented (overweight or obesity, prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL, or metabolic syndrome) to support MASLD.
Alternative causes are considered and excluded: viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
Aminotransferases are typically normal or only mildly elevated; an AST/ALT ratio above 1 suggests alcohol-associated disease or advanced fibrosis.
Noninvasive fibrosis assessment (FIB-4 or elastography) is performed because symptoms and enzyme levels do not predict stage.
Thrombocytopenia, low albumin, or elevated INR should prompt evaluation for advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis.
Red flags such as jaundice with confusion, hematemesis, or new ascites indicate decompensated disease and require urgent care.

easy: Middle-aged adult with obesity and type 2 diabetes
Incidentally elevated ALT on routine labs
Abdominal ultrasound showing a bright liver
No signs of chronic liver disease on exam
medium: Patient with both metabolic risk factors and moderate alcohol use, requiring careful attribution
AST/ALT ratio above 1 raising concern for alcohol-associated disease
Normal aminotransferases despite steatosis on imaging
Mild right upper quadrant discomfort with hepatomegaly
Need to exclude chronic hepatitis B or C before labeling as MASLD
hard: Older adult with thrombocytopenia and low albumin suggesting unrecognized cirrhosis
Young patient with steatosis and neuropsychiatric symptoms raising concern for Wilson disease
Elevated ferritin with high transferrin saturation suggesting hemochromatosis
Patient on amiodarone or methotrexate where drug-induced injury must be excluded
Pregnant patient with abnormal liver tests requiring distinction from acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Child with obesity and abdominal pain found to have steatosis
